Introduction

Education and healthcare are two powerful factors shaping the life qualities for women around the globe, but the relationship between them hugely varies by country based on different levels of development. During times when countries are trying to solve problems with education inequality, gaps in healthcare resources, and problematic gender stereotypes, it’s crucial to look at the question of how the level of education women receive can influence their health outcomes. From a macro perspective, global indicators had evident contrasts. We see this in the Average Birth Rate Per Country map below as it shows major regional disparities in fertility and health expenditure. These inequalities led to the central question of our project, which is “ How does women’s education shape reproductive, maternal, and overall health outcomes across countries?” To investigate this question, we as a team conducted research on the World Bank’s gender data portal to see the long-term trend of gender, health, and socioeconomic development. These datasets incorporated information and statistics from the United Nations and also the national statistical offices, as well as international health and labor organizations. This dataset is highly relevant to our research because it provides standardized and internationally comparable statistical data from 2000-2023. The datasets contained variables such as school enrollment, adolescent fertility, maternal healthcare access, gender parity indexes, and health expenditures. After thorough data cleaning and processing, we as a team applied Tableau and R software to do the graph visualizations. For example, scatterplots linking health expenditure, adolescent fertility, and birth rate. These data visualizations demonstrated that there’s a significant positive correlation between women’s level of education and their healthcare-related issues. The chosen dataset provided the foundation to our central thesis, that the investment for women’s education not only can improve their healthcare outcomes, but also promotes a broader level of socioeconomic welfare support.

Through our literature review, we have analyzed that scholars overwhelmingly agree that the structural, socioeconomic, and cultural circumstances of health continuously impact and deeply shape the way gender inequality in education, women’s health, and reproductive outcomes are presented and understood. For example, some researchers like O’Connor, Zeng, Singh, and Pezzulo highlight how institutional norms that have been in place for years, such as unequal resource distribution as well as patriarchal expectations, continue to limit women’s access to education and healthcare. In addition, the studies conducted by Azzopardi, Tamir, Ran, and Okui, show that when women and girls gain access to secondary schooling and health services, their overall health outcomes improve while fertility rates decline and risks such as maternal mortality and teenage pregnancy decrease. The scholars also agree that education operates as a catalyst to empower women with knowledge, expand economic opportunities, and improve infant and maternal health, which shows how there is a pattern and trend surrounding this topic. We believe this body of research in this literature demonstrates that gendered social conditions, not just biological differences, shape women’s and children’s health trajectories across developing countries. Although the literature consistently emphasizes the importance of education and socioeconomic conditions, that does not fully encompass the full picture, as contradictions and further exploration are necessary in some respects. When analyzing studies conducted by Addo and Stange, we noticed that they discuss the relationship between fertility timing and education is complex and is definitely influenced by pre-existing social factors that shape life paths even before childbearing occurs. We believe that some of the scholars who have been included rarely examine the long-term, non-reproductive health outcomes of women with lower education, which is an issue raised only by Saliba and Zurayk. We also noticed that there is limited research on how newer forms of access to information, such as internet connectivity, impact cultural norms to influence how women decide how to approach reproductive health. With everything that has been researched, we believe the literature has not necessarily explored how gendered health inequalities evolve across generations and how truly effective current policy interventions about local norms interact with global development agendas. These gaps suggest that there is a need for more intersectional, region-specific, and long-term research on the effects of education on health. With this, we need time, but we believe that with this literature review and research that we have conducted, we have gathered the most accurate information possible.

Our project is significant because it connects the global issue of education and healthcare inequalities with the authentic living experiences, narratives, and power dynamics that shape women’s reproductive health. While many previous research studies analyzed infant mortality rate with a country’s GDP and reproductive autonomy, not many investigations discussed how women’s access to high-quality education can intersect with these issues based on the diverse cultural backgrounds of different countries. Our analysis brings different perspectives together to demonstrate how educational opportunity, or the lack of it, can lead to how women’s health outcomes can be represented, both in statistics and narratives. Through combining a humanistic point of view and empirical health data, our group’s project illuminated how the differences in women’s power representation, structural inequalities, and unequal access to education opportunities can increase gaps in healthcare services. Especially in low-income or marginalized areas. Ultimately, we hope that this research project will push to enhance the knowledge of reproductive health around the globe in a more human-centered and education-focused approach.

What is the relationship between women’s participation in secondary education and birth rates in major developing countries?

The first visualization compares the female share of secondary education completion rates across low to middle-income countries in the years 2018 (top) and 2021 (bottom), ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births), where the left of the visualization indicates low infant mortality rates and the right side indicates high reports of infant mortality. Each bar reflects the proportion of secondary students who are female (green) versus male (yellow). The dashed line marks the 45% female-share threshold. Our group selected years 2018 and 2021 to demonstrate how the COVID-19 pandemic affected girls’ secondary education and infant mortality outcomes.

In 2018, it is important to note that the majority of countries just barely meet the 45% female share benchmark, but by 2021,nearly all in the dataset will exceed this standard. This indicates that access and retention of girls in secondary education greatly improved in the year 2021, following the height of the global pandemic, which called for an emphasis on the importance of education, whether that be virtual or in person(Tamir). Also, by the year 2021 is expected that Sierra Leone will have the highest infant mortality rate, and it will actually become the country with the highest share of secondary completion by females. This demonstrates a huge jump from 2018, where we see that secondary completion rates by females were at 49.5%. This suggests that progress was made in both female health and education fields following the global pandemic, especially due to the high mortality rates that it caused, and the awareness that it shed on preventative health care.

Additionally, while hovering over each bar, we can see the exact infant mortality rate for each country and note that the maximum infant mortality rate for Cape Verde has actually decreased from 58.2% to 54.0% after the pandemic. This could be due to a greater spotlight on education in low-income countries following the outbreak of COVID-19, which would support more online work instead of in-person work that low-income countries often partake in(Akanbi et al. 138–146) We also see a decline in infant mortality due to a greater focus on health, which is a result of more educational opportunities and emphasis.

Overall, this visualization illustrated how Covid-19 increased the attention coming from societies on the access to education. As a result there was evident improvement in these two fields. This positive trend followed by the past academic researches that the welfare for women can be significantly improved. (Okui; Pezzulo et al.) Education will make women better understand their reproductive system and more healthcare participation. In the meantime the risk for the pregnant women and the infant will be lower.

While visualization 1 explicitly highlighted how getting education can benefit the health of pregnant women and infants, visualization 2 moved its focus to an even earlier stage of life, shifting its focus to adolescent girls who might not have completed secondary school yet. This visualization helps the audience to understand the economic disadvantage (particularly the participation into the workforce for teenage people) and its relationship to fertility outcomes and literacy levels. These findings supported the wide range of investigations. For researchers such as Azzopardi et al., who emphasize that adolescent wellbeing is shaped by intertwined educational and economic struggles (Azzopardi et al. 1101–1118). Whereas authors such as Singh and Singh argued that the difference when it comes to getting resources due to gender difference can greatly influence a woman’s health conditions (Singh and Singh). From here, the audience can see that visualization 2 demonstrates that labor, education, and reproductive behavior can intersect with each other before a girl turns into an adult.

The visualization illustrates adolescent fertility rates (for females ages 15-24) for six bins of youth labor force participation in order to reveal important connections and relationships between adolescent girls between labor, education, and reproductive behavior. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin. The color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that specific labor-force-participation range. In the lowest labor force participation bin, adolescents demonstrate both the lowest average fertility rates and the lowest female-to-male literacy ratios. This suggests that entering and engaging in the workforce may be caused by restricted access to schooling that can thus suppress literacy and childbearing in adolescents. With limited education opportunities, it is linked with lower reproductive knowledge and influence childbearing patterns, consistent with findings from Azzopardi et al. and Akanbi et al., who link limited schooling to higher risks for teenage pregnancy (Akanbi et al. 138–146). Additionally, entering certain forms of work may not require or encourage formal schooling, which can further enforce poor literacy outcomes.

As labor force participation increases, average fertility rates increase slightly, but fertility outcomes vary the most, particularly in the 33.5–40.4 participation bin. This displays the greatest variability and can indicate that adolescents who enter the workforce at higher rates might be doing so at ages that experience close to or peak fertility years. The visualization illustrates that the highest labor force participation groups also happen to contain some of the highest fertility values. This goes against the idea that greater economic stability leads to delayed fertility amongst adolescent females. Instead, the visualization suggests that high adolescent labor participation may lead to early work and parenthood (Zeng et al.; Singh and Singh).

Overall the second visualization showcased the importance of understanding the relationship between adolescent labor behaviors in a broader social and economic contexts. That adolescent groups working is not only an economical indicator, but it’s highly related to literacy rates, access to education and giving birth to the next generation. This chart emphasized the core of our project, that education is a crucial indicator of the health status of women. The impact can be long standing even before adulthood.

This visualization explores and compares a country’s neonatal mortality rates versus the economic size (GDP) and the health expenditure that each country endows. This visualization in particular applies a log scale to GDP to reduce the extreme spread in values and allow patterns to be more easily interpreted. The results show that health expenditure per capita is far more strongly associated with neonatal mortality than GDP itself. The color gradient makes this clear: countries with higher health spending consistently exhibit lower neonatal mortality rates, regardless of their GDP level.

Interestingly, across the middle of the GDP distribution, we observe a concentration of countries—largely lower- to middle-income economies—with notably higher neonatal mortality rates. In contrast, both the lowest-GDP and highest-GDP countries show similar ranges of neonatal mortality outcomes, suggesting that GDP alone is not a reliable predictor of neonatal survival. This reinforces the idea that investment in health systems, rather than economic size, is what directly improves neonatal outcomes. Moreover, this also reinforces the idea that “higher-educated mothers have better access to healthcare services and resources, including quality antenatal care and skilled birth attendants, which can lead to timely interventions and improved neonatal outcomes” that are showcased through investment in healthcare systems. When women are more highly educated and have quality access to healthcare through increased health expenditure, neonatal mortality rates decrease, and overall reproductive and early childhood health increases.

The visualization therefore, highlights that increased health expenditure has a more immediate and measurable impact on reducing neonatal mortality than broad economic indicators. Policies that improve women’s access to healthcare, prenatal services, and skilled birth assistance can directly reduce neonatal mortality, even in countries with modest GDP levels.
